Langfuse upgrades its axios dependency to 1.8.2 due to the CVE-2025-27152.
Affected versions of the langfuse package are vulnerable to Open Redirect due to improper validation of user-controlled redirect paths in the client-side authentication flow.

Affected versions of the langfuse package are vulnerable to server-side request forgery (SSRF) due to webhook HTTP redirects not being validated against the same hostname/IP allow/deny rules as the original webhook URL.
Affected versions of the langfuse package are vulnerable to Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) due to missing validation of a user-configurable PostHog base URL/hostname.

Security Fix for Langfuse 3.28.1 | Security upgrades for DOMPurify and release-it dependencies.
- Fixed Versions: v3.28.1
- Affected Versions: <v3.28.1

DOMPurify is non-pypi

Affected versions of Langfuse are potentially vulnerable to hyperlink injection in organization invitation emails. An attacker controlling the invitedByUserEmail or inviteLink parameters could inject malicious anchor tags into the MembershipInvitationEmailTemplate.tsx, enabling phishing or social engineering attacks via content spoofing. These vulnerable Link components lacked proper encoding or sanitization, analogous to CWE-116 Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output vulnerabilities.
Langfuse has updated the nanoid dependency to version 3.3.8 across multiple package.json files to address a security vulnerability identified as CVE-2024-55565.

langgraph.advisory: Affected versions of the langgraph package are vulnerable to Deserialization of Untrusted Data due to unsafe msgpack checkpoint deserialization that can reconstruct Python objects from attacker-controlled checkpoint bytes. LangGraph checkpointers load msgpack-encoded checkpoints from the persistence layer, and when checkpoint data is tampered with, the checkpoint loading process can deserialize crafted payloads that trigger unsafe object reconstruction during resume operations.

langgraph-checkpoint.advisory: Affected versions of the langgraph-checkpoint package are vulnerable to Deserialization of Untrusted Data due to the “constructor” pathway in JsonPlusSerializer’s “json” mode that reconstructs arbitrary objects during deserialization. The langgraph.checkpoint.serde.jsonplus.JsonPlusSerializer.loads_typed() routine accepts payloads with lc==2 and type=="constructor" and resolves the id path to callables (for example ["os","system"]); moreover, when msgpack serialization fails on illegal Unicode surrogates the library falls back to “json,” allowing attacker-controlled checkpoint records to be executed on load.

Affected versions of the langgraph-checkpoint package are vulnerable to Deserialization of Untrusted Data due to unsafe pickle fallback deserialization in the default cache serializer. LangGraph’s BaseCache defaults to JsonPlusSerializer(pickle_fallback=True), and when msgpack serialization fails, JsonPlusSerializer.loads_typed(...) will deserialize cached entries marked as type "pickle" using pickle.loads(...), impacting cache backends inheriting from BaseCache (such as RedisCache and SqliteCache) when nodes opt into caching via CachePolicy.

langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite.advisory: Affected versions of the langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite package are vulnerable to SQL Injection due to direct string concatenation of user-controlled filter operators into SQL queries without parameterization. In LangGraph’s SQLite store implementation (langgraph.store.sqlite.base), the parsing of the $eq, $ne, $gt, $lt, $gte, and $lte operators feeds untrusted values into WHERE clauses via string concatenation instead of bound parameters, enabling malicious tokens to alter query structure.

Affected versions of the langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite package are vulnerable to SQL Injection due to the construction of SQL fragments using untrusted filter keys without proper parameterization. The SqliteStore.search method in langgraph.store.sqlite.base concatenates the user-controlled filter key into a json_extract() predicate (e.g., building the WHERE clause from the filter map) instead of using bound parameters, allowing crafted keys to modify the query logic and bypass access controls.

Affected versions of the pyrofork package are vulnerable to Path Traversal due to unsanitized attacker-controlled filenames being used in download paths in the download_media method. In pyrofork versions <= 2.3.68, download_media falls back to the Telegram-controlled media.file_name value when no explicit filename is supplied and then combines it with a base directory using os.path.join and os.path.abspath without stripping dot-dot-dash sequences or absolute paths, allowing temp_file_path to resolve outside the intended download directory.

langroid.advisory: Affected versions of Langroid are vulnerable to Code Injection when using TableChatAgent. TableChatAgent uses pandas eval(). If fed by untrusted user input, like the case of a public-facing LLM application, an attacker may be able to make the agent run malicious commands compromising the host system.

Affected versions of Langroid are vulnerable to Code Injection when using LanceDocChatAgent. LanceDocChatAgent uses pandas eval() through compute_from_docs(). As a result, an attacker may be able to make the agent run malicious commands through QueryPlan.dataframe_calc compromising the host system.

Affected versions of the Langroid package are vulnerable to XML External Entity (XXE) Injection through the XMLToolMessage class. The XMLToolMessage.extract() method fails to properly configure the lxml parser with security safeguards, allowing processing of malicious XML entities and DTDs. 

A remote attacker can exploit this vulnerability by sending specially crafted XML input containing entity expansion attacks (billion laughs) or external entity references, resulting in denial of service through memory exhaustion or unauthorized disclosure of local files with sensitive information.

The vulnerability was fixed by hardening the XMLParser initialization with security flags that disable entity resolution (resolve_entities=False), DTD loading (load_dtd=False), network access (no_network=True), and external entity processing (dtd_validation=False, dtd_attrs=False).

Affected versions of the langroid package are vulnerable to Remote Code Execution due to an incomplete WAF used to restrict pandas expression evaluation. The TableChatAgent pandas_eval tool in langroid/agent/special/table_chat_agent.py relies on the WAF logic in langroid/utils/pandas_utils.py, but _literal_ok() returns False instead of raising UnsafeCommandError and still permits access to dangerous dunder attributes such as __init__, __globals__, and __builtins__, enabling attackers to recover the eval builtin through chained whitelisted DataFrame methods.

Affected versions of the langroid package are vulnerable to SQL Injection leading to Remote Code Execution due to the absence of query validation in the SQLChatAgent component. The run_query method in sql_chat_agent.py executes LLM-generated SQL statements directly against the configured database without parsing or restricting the allowed statement types. An attacker who can influence the agent's input, including indirectly through prompt injection via data returned to the LLM, can coerce execution of dangerous database primitives such as PostgreSQL's COPY FROM PROGRAM to achieve arbitrary command execution on the database host.

langsmith.advisory: Langsmith 0.1.84 removes its lodash.set dependency because the package is no longer maintained. Using the lodash library instead is recommended, which continues to receive updates and maintenance.

Affected versions of the langsmith package are vulnerable to Deserialization of Untrusted Data due to the absence of a trust boundary distinction when pulling public prompt manifests from the LangSmith Hub. The pull_prompt, pull_prompt_commit (Python) and pullPrompt, pullPromptCommit (JS/TS) methods fetch and deserialise prompt manifests that may contain serialised LangChain Runnable or PromptTemplate objects with attacker-controlled constructor kwargs, as well as model configuration such as custom base_url, default headers, and model name, without validating whether the manifest originates from a trusted source.

Affected versions of the langsmith package are vulnerable to Deserialization of Untrusted Data due to the absence of a trust boundary distinction when pulling public prompt manifests from the LangSmith Hub. The pull_prompt, pull_prompt_commit (Python), and pullPrompt, pullPromptCommit (JS/TS) methods fetch and deserialise prompt manifests that may contain serialised LangChain Runnable or PromptTemplate objects with attacker-controlled constructor kwargs, as well as model configuration such as custom base_url, default headers, and model name, without validating whether the manifest originates from a trusted source.

Affected versions of the langsmith package are vulnerable to Information Disclosure because the output redaction pipeline is not applied to streaming token events. The hide_outputs control in the Python SDK is implemented by _hide_run_outputs at run_helpers.py lines 1924 and 1996, which only processes the inputs and outputs fields on a run and never the events array, so new_token events containing raw kwargs.token values are recorded during streaming without redaction. Applications that rely on output redaction to prevent sensitive LLM output from being stored in LangSmith will still leak the full streamed content via run events, exposing content that the redaction configuration was intended to suppress.

Affected versions of the langsmith package are vulnerable to Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) due to accepting attacker-controlled replica configuration values from the baggage tracing header without validation. In distributed tracing, RunTree.from_headers() (Python) and RunTree.fromHeaders() (TypeScript) parse the baggage header and previously allowed embedded api_url values, after which the SDK’s post() and patch() methods transmit run data to every configured replica URL.

language-formatters-pre-commit-hooks.advisory:
Language-formatters-pre-commit-hooks 1.6.0 enhances its security in commands execution  to prevent shell-injection.

language-pipes.advisory: Affected versions of this package are vulnerable to Use of a Predictable IV. The _bind() method in lemur/auth/ldap.py invokes ldap.set_option(ldap.OPT_X_TLS_REQUIRE_CERT, ldap.OPT_X_TLS_NEVER) at the global module level, which disables certificate validation for the entire Python process and accepts self-signed, expired, hostname-mismatched, and revoked certificates without any override option.

Affected versions of the lemur package are vulnerable to LDAP Injection due to unsanitised user input being interpolated directly into LDAP search filters. The _bind() method in lemur/auth/ldap.py constructs the user lookup filter "userPrincipalName=%s" from the username submitted to POST /auth/login and the Active Directory group filter "(&(objectclass=group)(member:1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941:={}))" from the resulting userdn without ever calling ldap.filter.escape_filter_chars(). The file lightrag/api/config.py at line 397 falls back to the publicly known string "lightrag-jwt-default-secret", and the AuthHandler in lightrag/api/auth.py uses this secret to sign and verify tokens at lines 24-25. An unauthenticated attacker can forge valid JWT tokens using the known default secret and gain unauthorised access to any protected API endpoint.

Affected versions of the lightrag-hku package are vulnerable to Authentication Bypass (JWT Algorithm Confusion) due to the validate_token method in lightrag/api/auth.py not explicitly denying the none algorithm when calling jwt.decode(). The jwt.decode() call at line 128 accepts the algorithm specified in the token header, allowing a crafted JWT with alg set to none and no signature to be processed as valid. An attacker can forge arbitrary JWT tokens, including those with admin-level claims, to gain full unauthorised access to all protected API endpoints without valid credentials.

litdb.advisory: Affected versions of the litdb package are vulnerable to Remote Code Execution due to unsafe use of Python’s eval() when parsing default values in the schema DSL. The parse_schema_dsl function in src/litdb/extract.py evaluated the user-controlled default_str via eval without validation, enabling arbitrary Python expressions to be executed during schema parsing; the fixing commit replaces eval with ast.literal_eval for safe literal parsing.

litellm.advisory: BerriAI/litellm is vulnerable to Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) via the /completions endpoint. The vulnerability arises from the hf_chat_template method processing the chat_template parameter from the tokenizer_config.json file through the Jinja template engine without proper sanitization. Attackers can exploit this by crafting malicious tokenizer_config.json files that execute arbitrary code on the server.

Litellm version 1.35.1.dev1 introduces a low-severity security fix by disabling demo accounts on the Admin UI. Previously, the Proxy used a hardcoded demo account with no permissions, posing a potential security risk.
Affected versions of Litellm are vulnerable to improper authorization. Users could remove files from litellm proxy server when calling  /audio/transcriptions.

Affected versions of BerriAI's litellm are vulnerable to arbitrary file deletion due to improper input validation on the `/audio/transcriptions` endpoint. An attacker can exploit this vulnerability by sending a specially crafted request that includes a file path to the server, which then deletes the specified file without proper authorization or validation. This vulnerability is present in the code where `os.remove(file.filename)` is used to delete a file, allowing any user to delete critical files on the server such as SSH keys, SQLite databases, or configuration files.
Litellm version 1.35.20.dev2 resolves an issue where users could inadvertently delete files from the Litellm proxy server when accessing the `/audio/transcriptions` endpoint.

berriai/litellm affected versions are vulnerable to improper access control in their team management functionality. This vulnerability allows attackers to perform unauthorized actions such as creating, updating, viewing, deleting, blocking, and unblocking any team, as well as adding or deleting any member to or from any teams. The vulnerability stems from insufficient access control checks in various team management endpoints, enabling attackers to exploit these functionalities without proper authorization.
Affected version of Litellm are affected by a information disclosure vulnerability. Sensitive information was logged in raw request debug logs.

Affected versions of berriai/litellm contain a Code Injection vulnerability (CWE-94) in the secret management system when using Google KMS. Attackers could potentially execute arbitrary code by manipulating environment variables, exploiting the use of eval() on unvalidated input. This vulnerability has been addressed by replacing eval() with a secure client.decrypt() method for handling encrypted data.

Affected versions of berriai/litellm contains a Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerability (CWE-94) in the secret management system, particularly when using Google KMS. The litellm.get_secret() method used the eval() function unsafely on unsanitized input from environment variables, which could be manipulated through the /config/update endpoint. This allowed attackers to inject and execute arbitrary code by updating settings in proxy_server_config.yaml. The vulnerability has been addressed by replacing the unsafe eval() call with a secure client.decrypt() method for handling encrypted data.

Affected versions of the litellm package are vulnerable to Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks due to insufficient validation of request body parameters. The api_base and base_url fields in POST /chat/completions requests are not properly restricted, allowing attackers to redirect server-side API calls to attacker-controlled domains.
This vulnerability permits malicious users to exfiltrate sensitive data—including OpenAI API keys—by proxying requests through untrusted endpoints. Exploitation may result in unauthorized access to third-party services, data leakage, or misuse of exposed secrets.

**Advisory Correction Notice:**
The original advisory states that this vulnerability was fixed in version v1.44.8. However, following a thorough analysis, Safety’s Cyber Research team has confirmed that a fix for this vulnerability is actually available in versions v1.44.9 and onwards. The fix was introduced in the following [commit](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/commit/ba1912afd1b19e38d3704bb156adf887f91ae1e0). This corrects the version information implied by the original advisory.

Affected versions of Litellm are vulnerable to blind SQL Injection. This vulnerability in the '/team/update' endpoint allows attackers to inject malicious SQL commands through the 'user_id' parameter, potentially leading to unauthorized access to sensitive data including API keys, user information, and tokens. The flaw stems from improper handling of user input in raw SQL queries. The patch replaces vulnerable raw SQL queries with parameterized queries using Prisma ORM, effectively preventing SQL injection attacks.

Affected versions of the litellm package are vulnerable to Information Disclosure due to improper error handling in team settings parsing. The proxy_server.py module exposes sensitive Langfuse API keys, including langfuse_secret and langfuse_public_key, in error messages when team settings parsing fails.

A vulnerability in BerriAI/litellm, as of commit 26c03c9, allows unauthenticated users to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) by exploiting the use of ast.literal_eval to parse user input. This function is not safe and is prone to DoS attacks, which can crash the litellm Python server.
LiteLLM has addressed the security vulnerability CVE-2024-22020 by updating the Node.js Docker image from version 20.11.0 to 20.18.1.
Litellm 1.56.2 updates its dependency 'cryptography' to include a security fix.

A Denial of Service (DoS) vulnerability exists in berriai/litellm version v1.44.5. This vulnerability can be exploited by appending characters, such as dashes (-), to the end of a multipart boundary in an HTTP request. The server continuously processes each character, leading to excessive resource consumption and rendering the service unavailable. The issue is unauthenticated and does not require any user interaction, impacting all users of the service.

A sensitive security token was inadvertently exposed in the Hugging Face models metadata file (CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information), risking unauthorized access. Litellm fixing it by removing the token-containing entry, preventing potential misuse.
Litellm fixes a vulnerability where a user could update another user's keys.
Litellm 1.61.20 includes a security fix: Enforce model access restrictions on Azure OpenAI route.

Affected versions of the spend_management_endpoints.py were potentially vulnerable to SQL Injection (CWE-89). An attacker could potentially inject malicious SQL code through unsanitized input, leading to unauthorized data access or manipulation. The issue exists in the spend_management_endpoints.py.
Litellm Fixes potential SQL Injection in spend_management_endpoints.py.

Affected versions of the litellm package are vulnerable to Improper Access Control due to incomplete role-based authorization checks on management routes. The _check_proxy_admin_viewer_access function in litellm/proxy/auth/route_checks.py did not consistently block write operations for the PROXY_ADMIN_VIEW_ONLY role on endpoints such as /key/generate, /key/update, and user/team/model routes, and management_endpoints/internal_user_endpoints._update_single_user_helper lacked a can_user_call_user_update guard to restrict updates to self or PROXY_ADMIN.

Affected versions of the litellm package are vulnerable to Information Disclosure due to missing authentication on sensitive in-memory cache debug endpoints. The /memory-usage-in-mem-cache and /memory-usage-in-mem-cache-items routes in litellm/proxy/common_utils/debug_utils.py lacked the Depends(user_api_key_auth) check and were not initially listed under master_key_only_routes in litellm/proxy/_types.py, which permitted unauthenticated inspection of cache information.

Affected versions of the litellm package before 69a464f are potentially vulnerable to Information Disclosure due to incomplete masking of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) secret fields in responses from the /models and /v1/models endpoints. The proxy’s model-listing path serializes the litellm_params structure and, before this change, remove_sensitive_info_from_deployment in proxy/common_utils/openai_endpoint_utils.py did not run SensitiveDataMasker.mask_dict on OCI-specific keys (for example key, tenancy, fingerprint, and key_file), causing those secrets to be returned unredacted.

Affected versions of the litellm package are potentially vulnerable to Information Disclosure due to the insertion of JWT SSO tokens and other credentials into info-level log messages. In litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/ui_sso.py (get_redirect_response_from_openid) and litellm/proxy/pass_through_endpoints/pass_through_endpoints.py (forward_upstream_to_client), logger.info statements recorded jwt_token and related authentication data in plaintext, a logging behaviour the project explicitly fixed and added tests for in tests/code_coverage_tests/info_log_check.py.
Affected versions of the litellm package are vulnerable to sensitive information exposure due to improper masking of raw request headers on /health endpoint failures.

Affected versions of this package are vulnerable to information disclosure due to improper handling of expired keys. The vulnerability exists because expired key plaintexts were being leaked in error responses. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by triggering error responses that inadvertently reveal sensitive expired key information, potentially leading to unauthorized access or misuse of the disclosed keys.

Affected versions of the litellm package are vulnerable to sensitive information exposure due to insufficient sanitization of guardrail logging data. The add_standard_logging_guardrail_information_to_request_data path in litellm/integrations/custom_guardrail.py logged guardrail responses without removing secret_fields, which could include raw_headers.authorization, and the issue was fixed in commit 7e60e22.
https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/pull/23162

Affected versions of the litellm package are vulnerable to information exposure because they store Presidio PII tokens in a top-level request field that could be forwarded to providers. The Presidio guardrail logic in litellm/proxy/guardrails/guardrail_hooks/presidio.py stored pii_tokens directly in request_data instead of under request_data["metadata"], which allowed those token mappings to leak to strict providers such as Anthropic. The fix landed in commit 861db11.
https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/pull/22627

Affected versions of the LiteLLM package are vulnerable to privilege escalation due to missing authorization checks on key-management endpoints. The /key/block, /key/unblock, and /key/update handlers allowed INTERNAL_USER callers to act on arbitrary keys or raise max_budget without enforcing proxy-admin, team-admin, org-admin, or ownership checks; the fix was merged in commit bc810f9.
https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/pull/23781

Affected versions of the litellm package are vulnerable to Authentication Bypass due to weak unsalted SHA-256 password hashing combined with exposure of password hashes through multiple API endpoints. The /user/info, /user/update, and /spend/users endpoints return password hash fields to any authenticated user, and the /v2/login endpoint accepts raw SHA-256 hashes directly without re-hashing, enabling a pass-the-hash attack. An authenticated user can retrieve another user’s password hash from any of these endpoints and use it to log in as that user, achieving full privilege escalation in as few as three HTTP requests.

Affected versions of the litellm package are vulnerable to Authentication Bypass due to the use of an insufficiently unique cache key derived from only the first 20 characters of a JWT token in the OIDC userinfo cache. When JWT authentication is enabled, the cache key is computed as token[:20], and because JWT headers produced by the same signing algorithm generate identical prefixes, an attacker can craft a token whose first 20 characters collide with a legitimate cached entry. This allows an unauthenticated attacker to inherit the identity and permissions of a legitimate user on cache hit, resulting in full authentication bypass on deployments with JWT/OIDC authentication enabled.

Affected versions of the litellm package are vulnerable to Privilege Escalation due to missing admin role authorisation on the /config/update endpoint. This endpoint allows any authenticated user to modify proxy configuration and environment variables, register custom pass-through endpoint handlers pointing to attacker-controlled Python code, read arbitrary server files via the UI_LOGO_PATH setting, and overwrite privileged account credentials by modifying UI_USERNAME and UI_PASSWORD environment variables. An authenticated low-privilege attacker can exploit this endpoint to achieve Remote Code Execution, read sensitive server files, or take over administrator accounts without requiring proxy_admin role privileges.

Affected versions of the litellm package are vulnerable to Remote Code Execution due to unsafe evaluation of decrypted environment variables. The `add_deployment` function in litellm versions before 1.40.16 decodes and decrypts base64-encoded values using Google KMS, then assigns them directly to `os.environ` without sanitization, enabling injection of malicious code. A remote attacker can exploit this by sending a crafted payload via the `/config/update` endpoint, triggering `get_secret` and executing arbitrary code in the litellm process with full privileges.

Affected versions of the litellm package are vulnerable to SQL Injection attacks due to improper input sanitization. The /global/spend/logs endpoint constructs an SQL query by directly concatenating the unvalidated api_key parameter into the query string without escaping or parameterization. This allows attackers to inject arbitrary SQL code by supplying specially crafted input through the api_key parameter. Successful exploitation may lead to unauthorized data access, manipulation of database contents, exposure of sensitive information, or a Denial of Service (DoS) condition.

Affected versions of the litellm package are vulnerable to Information Disclosure due to improper redaction of API keys in logging output. The litellm_logging.py file within the litellm_core_utils module attempts to mask API keys but only obfuscates the first five characters, inadvertently exposing nearly the entire key in logs.
This vulnerability can be exploited when API requests are logged by the application, leaking sensitive credentials to log files and increasing the risk of unauthorized access if the logs are accessed by an attacker or improperly secured.

BerriAI/litellm version 1.40.12 contains a vulnerability that allows remote code execution. The issue exists in the handling of the 'postcallrules' configuration, where a callback function can be added. The provided value is split at the final '.' mark, with the last part considered the function name and the remaining part appended with the '.py' extension and imported. This allows an attacker to set a system method, such as 'os.system', as a callback, enabling the execution of arbitrary commands when a chat response is processed.

An improper authorization vulnerability exists in the main-latest version of BerriAI/litellm. When a user with the role 'internal_user_viewer' logs into the application, they are provided with an overly privileged API key. This key can be used to access all the admin functionality of the application, including endpoints such as '/users/list' and '/users/get_users'. This vulnerability allows for privilege escalation within the application, enabling any account to become a PROXY ADMIN.

Affected versions of the litellm package are vulnerable to OS Command Injection due to authenticated MCP preview endpoints accepting attacker-supplied stdio transport configuration without authorization checks. The endpoints POST /mcp-rest/test/connection and POST /mcp-rest/test/tools/list accept a full MCP server configuration in the request body, including the command, args, and env fields, and when invoked with a stdio configuration they spawn the supplied command as a subprocess on the proxy host with the privileges of the proxy process, gated only by a valid proxy API key with no role check. Any authenticated user, including holders of low-privilege internal-user keys, can therefore execute arbitrary commands on the proxy host, resulting in full remote code execution under the proxy service account.

Affected versions of the litellm package are vulnerable to Server-Side Template Injection due to the POST /prompts/test endpoint rendering user-supplied prompt templates without sandboxing. The endpoint only verifies that the caller presents a valid proxy API key, so any authenticated user can submit a crafted template that is rendered in an unrestricted template environment and thereby execute arbitrary code inside the LiteLLM Proxy process. An attacker with a valid proxy API key can exploit this to run commands on the host and read secrets from the process environment, including provider API keys and database credentials, leading to full compromise of the proxy deployment.

Affected versions of the litellm package are vulnerable to SQL Injection due to caller-supplied proxy API key values being concatenated into the database query text used during proxy API key verification instead of being passed as a separate parameter. Unauthenticated input from the Authorization header on any LLM API route, such as POST /chat/completions, reaches the vulnerable query through the proxy's error-handling path, allowing attacker-controlled SQL syntax to alter the intended statement. An unauthenticated attacker can exploit this by sending a specially crafted Authorization header to read data from the proxy's database and may be able to modify it, resulting in unauthorised access to the proxy and the credentials it manages.

Affected versions of the litellm package are vulnerable to Sandbox Escape due to an insufficient hand-rolled sandbox in the custom-code guardrail testing endpoint. The POST /guardrails/test_custom_code endpoint executes user-supplied Python code within a custom sandbox that can be bypassed using bytecode-level techniques, allowing arbitrary code execution in the proxy process. An attacker with proxy-admin credentials can escape the sandbox to achieve arbitrary code execution, which runs as root in the default Docker image.

Affected versions of the litellm package are vulnerable to Embedded Malicious Code due to a compromised PyPI publishing path that allowed attacker-supplied releases to be uploaded to the package index. In version 1.82.7, the malicious payload was embedded in litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py and triggered on import litellm.proxy, while version 1.82.8 additionally introduced litellm_init.pth, causing the payload to run at Python startup, collect credentials and sensitive files, and exfiltrate them to https://models.litellm.cloud/. An attacker can exploit this by tricking a user or build system into installing and running versions 1.82.7 or 1.82.8, resulting in theft of environment variables, cloud credentials, SSH keys, and other secrets available on the affected host.

litestar.advisory: Affected versions of the litestar package are vulnerable to Denial of Service (DoS) due to unbounded memory allocation when parsing request bodies. The Request methods for parsing JSON, msgpack, and form-data content types use `await self.body()` to read the entire request stream into memory without implementing size limits or validation checks, while the multipart parser expects the complete request body as a single byte string by design. An attacker can exploit this vulnerability by sending extremely large requests with matching content types (such as using `curl -F "foo=</dev/random"` for multipart/form-data), causing the server to consume excessive amounts of memory until all available memory and swap space are exhausted, resulting in service unavailability.

Affected versions of the litestar package are vulnerable to Improper Output Neutralization for Logs due to unescaped incorporation of a user-controlled URL path into exception log messages. In litestar/logging/config.py, the _default_exception_logging_handler formats scope["path"] into the string "Uncaught exception (connection_type=%s, path=%s)" using %s rather than a neutralized representation (changed to %r in the fix), allowing CRLF sequences in the path to be written verbatim when exception logging is enabled (e.g., debug level or log_exceptions="always"). An unauthenticated attacker can send requests with %0d%0a embedded in the request path to inject newlines and forge Litestar log entries, enabling audit log spoofing and obfuscation of malicious activity.

Affected versions of the litestar package are vulnerable to Improper Input Validation due to unconditional trust of the X-Forwarded-For header when deriving the client identity for rate limiting. The RateLimitMiddleware uses cache_key_from_request() to build the rate-limit key and, if X-Forwarded-For is present, incorporates its value without validating that it originated from a trusted proxy, allowing arbitrary per-request IP spoofing.

Affected versions of the litestar package are vulnerable to Improper Input Validation due to AllowedHosts allowlist entries being converted into regular expressions without escaping regex metacharacters. In litestar.middleware.allowed_hosts, AllowedHostsConfig compiles allowed_hosts patterns into regexes where characters like . retain special meaning, so a literal entry such as example.com can incorrectly match non-literal Host header values such as exampleXcom.

Affected versions of the litestar package are vulnerable to Improper Input Validation due to non-injective cache key canonicalization that allows filename collisions. The litestar.stores.file._safe_file_name() routine applies unicodedata.normalize("NFKD", name) and then concatenates characters or str(ord(c)) for non-alphanumerics without delimiters, so distinct keys such as "k-" and "k45" (or "K" and "K") can map to the same on-disk filename when FileStore is used as a response-cache backend.

Affected versions of the litestar package are vulnerable to Improper Input Validation due to allowed CORS origins being compiled into a regular expression without escaping metacharacters. The litestar.config.cors.CORSConfig.allowed_origins_regex value is built from allow_origins entries and then validated with allowed_origins_regex.fullmatch(origin), which allows characters like . in an allowlisted origin to act as regex wildcards rather than literal dots.

Affected versions of Litestar are vulnerable to Path Traversal. This vulnerability allows attackers to exploit path traversal flaws, enabling unauthorized access to sensitive files outside the designated directories. Such access can lead to the disclosure of sensitive information or potentially compromise the server.

litestar-vite.advisory: Affected versions of the litestar-vite package are vulnerable to sensitive information exposure due to echoing request cookies into redirect responses. The redirect response classes in the Inertia integration previously passed cookies=request.cookies, causing client cookies to be reflected via response cookie handling.

Affected versions of the litestar-vite package are vulnerable to open redirect due to missing same-origin validation on redirect targets. The InertiaBack redirect logic trusts the Referer header and InertiaRedirect accepts a redirect_to parameter without validating that the resulting URL is same-origin/relative, which was addressed by adding a _get_redirect_url() validator in fix commit 5fbdf3248b193ea852cb4454305f8b708c9f9340.
