pyload.advisory: Affected versions of pyload are vulnerable to Open Redirection (CWE-601). This vulnerability allows attackers to redirect users to malicious sites by exploiting the improper handling of the next parameter in the login functionality. The attack vector involves crafting URLs with malicious next parameters, leading users to phishing or harmful websites. Vulnerable functions include login in app_blueprint.py and get_redirect_url in helpers.py. To mitigate, upgrade to pyload version which implements proper validation and handling of redirect URLs, preventing unauthorized redirections.

pyload is an open-source Download Manager written in pure Python. An authenticated user can change the download folder and upload a crafted template to the specified folder lead to remote code execution. There is no fix available at the time of publication. See CVE-2024-32880.

pyload-ng.advisory: An unsafe JavaScript evaluation vulnerability in pyLoad’s CAPTCHA processing code allows unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code in the client browser and potentially the backend server. Exploitation requires no user interaction or authentication and can result in session hijacking, credential theft, and full system rce.

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to Information Disclosure due to the global WebUI exception handler embedding full Python tracebacks into the rendered error response. The unauthenticated route /web/path:filename defined in src/pyload/webui/app/blueprints/app_blueprint.py passes attacker-controlled template names into render_template, and the handler in src/pyload/webui/app/handlers.py appends traceback.format_exc() output to the messages list which is iterated and printed by the modern theme base template. A remote unauthenticated attacker can request a non-existent template to reliably trigger a server exception and recover internal stack frames, source paths, and exception metadata, exposing implementation details that aid in mapping application internals and improving the reliability of follow-on attacks.

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to Server-Side Request Forgery due to incomplete remediation of an earlier private-IP filtering issue. The parse_urls API in src/pyload/core/api/__init__.py validates the supplied hostname through is_global_host() but then calls request_factory.get_url(), which instantiates HTTPRequest with allow_private_ip=True by default; the _pre_request_callback short-circuits when this flag is set, while pycurl is configured with FOLLOWLOCATION enabled and up to ten redirects. An authenticated attacker with ADD permission can host a server that responds with a 302 redirect to internal addresses such as 169.254.169.254, causing pyload-ng to follow the redirect and disclose cloud metadata and other private network responses.
Pyload-ng 0.5.0b3.dev31 includes a fix for CVE-2023-0297: Code Injection in GitHub repository pyload/pyload prior to 0.5.0b3.dev31.

Pyload-ng versions before 0.5.0b3.dev77 are vulnerable to Log Injection, allowing any unauthenticated actor to inject arbitrary messages into the logs gathered by 'pyload'. Forged or otherwise, corrupted log files can be used to cover an attacker’s tracks or even to implicate another party in the commission of a malicious act.

Pyload-ng versions before 0.5.0b3.dev77 are vulnerable to Unauthenticated Flask Configuration Leakage. Any unauthenticated user can browse to a specific URL to expose the Flask config, including the 'SECRET_KEY' variable.

The pyload API, which supports making API calls through GET requests, was vulnerable to significant security risks due to the session cookie not being set to SameSite: strict. This vulnerability exposed the library to potential Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks, enabling unauthenticated users to make any API call through such an attack. This security concern has been resolved in the release 0.5.0b3.dev78.
https://github.com/pyload/pyload/security/advisories/GHSA-pgpj-v85q-h5fm

Affected versions of pyLoad are vulnerable to path traversal via the storage_folder configuration setting. This vulnerability allows attackers to write files to arbitrary locations by manipulating the storage_folder path, potentially leading to arbitrary file writes and code execution. The vulnerability exists in the Core.init and Api.set_config_value functions where storage paths aren't properly validated. Attackers with access to configuration settings can exploit this through the web interface. Users should update to the version which implements proper path validation and restriction checks.

Affected versions of the pyLoad-ng package are vulnerable to Path Traversal due to insufficient sanitization of the package parameter in the CNL blueprint. The /addcrypted endpoint in src/pyload/webui/app/blueprints/cnl_blueprint.py constructs file paths using user-supplied input without properly validating directory traversal sequences, only removing forward slashes, backslashes, and colons while leaving path traversal patterns intact. An unauthenticated attacker can exploit this vulnerability by sending a specially crafted POST request with a malicious package parameter containing directory traversal sequences to write arbitrary files to the system, including cron jobs or systemd services, achieving remote code execution as root.

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to SQL Injection due to unsanitized concatenation of user-controlled input into a database query. The /json/add_package API path propagates the add_links parameter to src/pyload/core/database/file_database.py:update_link_info, which constructs a comma-separated list of URLs and interpolates it directly into SELECT id FROM links WHERE url IN ('{statuses}') rather than using parameterised placeholders, allowing crafted values to alter the SQL syntax. An authenticated attacker can send a POST request to /json/add_package with a malicious add_links value that terminates the string literal and injects arbitrary SQL, enabling modification or deletion of database records and causing data loss and service disruption in pyload-ng.

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to Code Injection due to unsanitized parameters in the Captcha script handler and the Click'N'Load (CNL) blueprint of the web interface. The CNL /flash/addcrypted2 endpoint and related handlers accept user-controlled fields such as the jk and package parameters and propagate them into the UI without proper validation or encoding, enabling attacker-supplied JavaScript to be injected and executed in the client browser.

Affected versions of the pyLoad package are vulnerable to Denial of Service (DoS) attacks due to insufficient validation of JavaScript code in the Click'n'Load (CNL) Blueprint handler. The `/flash/addcrypted2` endpoint accepts a `jk` parameter containing JavaScript code that is directly passed to the `eval_js()` function, which executes it through either `dukpy.evaljs()` or `js2py.eval_js()` without any timeout or resource limitations.

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to Path Traversal due to the use of os.path.commonprefix() instead of os.path.commonpath() in the _safe_extractall() function within src/pyload/plugins/extractors/UnTar.py. The commonprefix() function performs character-level string comparison rather than path-level comparison, so a tar archive member named to share a common string prefix with the extraction directory will incorrectly pass the traversal check at line 14. An attacker who hosts a specially crafted tar archive can write files to arbitrary sibling directories of the intended extraction path when a user downloads and extracts the archive with the ExtractArchive addon enabled.

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to Authorisation Bypass due to a mismatch between option names in the ADMIN_ONLY_CORE_OPTIONS set and the actual configuration option names for SSL certificate and key file paths. The set_config_value() function in src/pyload/core/api/init.py defines admin-only guards using the names ssl_cert and ssl_key, whereas the actual configuration options are ssl_certfile, ssl_keyfile, and ssl_certchain, causing the authorisation check to always evaluate to false for these options. A non-admin user with SETTINGS permission can overwrite the SSL certificate and key file paths to attacker-controlled values, enabling Man-in-the-Middle interception of all HTTPS traffic and credential theft after a server restart.

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to Improper Authentication due to reliance on a user-controllable Host header in a local-only access check. The @local_check decorator in src/pyload/webui/app/blueprints/cnl_blueprint.py protects the Click'N'Load routes, including /flash/, /flash/<id>, /flash/add, /flash/addcrypted, /flash/addcrypted2, /flashgot, /flashgot_pyload, and /flash/checkSupportForUrl, but it incorrectly trusts HTTP_HOST alongside REMOTE_ADDR, allowing a spoofed Host: 127.0.0.1:9666 header to satisfy the origin check.

pyLoad is an open-source Download Manager written in pure Python. There is an open redirect vulnerability due to incorrect validation of input values when redirecting users after login. pyLoad is validating URLs via the `get_redirect_url` function when redirecting users at login. This vulnerability has been patched with commit fe94451. See CVE-2024-24808.
pyLoad 0.5.0 is vulnerable to Unrestricted File Upload.

An authenticated user can change the download folder and upload a crafted template to the specified folder, leading to remote code execution.
### References
https://github.com/pyload/pyload/commit/249c41bd427fde87715e24a5fa3e7d5d63ae3312

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to Incorrect Authorisation due to a permission mismatch between WebUI JSON endpoints and the core API methods they invoke. The /json/package_order and /json/link_order routes in json_blueprint.py enforce only the ADD permission while the underlying order_package() and order_file() API methods require MODIFY, and /json/abort_link enforces DELETE while stop_downloads() requires MODIFY. An authenticated user with only ADD or DELETE permissions can invoke MODIFY-restricted operations such as reordering packages and files or aborting active downloads, achieving horizontal privilege escalation beyond their assigned role.

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to Deserialization of Untrusted Data because the storage_folder configuration option is omitted from the ADMIN_ONLY_OPTIONS set, and its existing path check fails to cover the Flask filesystem session directory. In src/pyload/core/api/init.py, the storage_folder realpath check blocks paths inside PKGDIR and userdir but not the Flask session store at /tmp/pyLoad/flask, allowing a non-admin user with SETTINGS and ADD permissions to redirect downloads into that directory and plant a malicious pickle payload under the deterministic filename md5('session:' + session_id) consumed by cachelib FileSystemCache's pickle.load(). Any subsequent HTTP request carrying the corresponding pyload_session cookie causes the crafted session file to be deserialized, yielding unauthenticated arbitrary code execution in the context of the pyload service process.

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to Path Traversal due to non-recursive string-replacement sanitization of package folder names. The add_package function in src/pyload/core/api/init.py sanitizes the supplied folder name through chained string replacement calls that strip parent-directory sequences and path separator characters, but each replacement runs only once, so an input that nests parent-directory tokens within additional dot and slash characters collapses into a value that still contains residual parent-directory sequences, which the operating system later resolves during file operations.

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to Code Injection due to improper control of code generation via a JS2PY sandbox escape in the handling of input passed to the `/flash/addcrypted2` API endpoint. The `/flash/addcrypted2` endpoint uses js2py—which suffers from a sandbox escape via CVE-2024-28397—and the endpoint’s localhost restriction can be bypassed using crafted HTTP headers, allowing execution of arbitrary shell commands within the code evaluation context. An attacker can send a request containing a shell command to the `/flash/addcrypted2` endpoint (even remotely by spoofing headers), resulting in remote code execution on the server, with high confidentiality, integrity, and availability impact.
Any unauthenticated attacker can bypass the localhost restrictions posed by the application and utilize this to create arbitrary packages.

Affected versions of the pyload package are vulnerable to Log Injection. The `/json/add_package` API endpoint fails to properly escape newline characters in package names, leading to arbitrary log entry injection. A user with add packages permission can exploit this vulnerability by crafting a package name containing newline characters and malicious log entries, resulting in corrupted log files that can be used to cover an attacker's tracks or implicate other parties in malicious acts.

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) due to missing URL destination validation. The /api/addPackage endpoint in src/pyload/webui/app/blueprints/api_blueprint.py accepts user-controlled values from the add_links parameter and passes them to api.add_package(name, links, dest), after which the download logic in src/pyload/core/managers/download.py fetches arbitrary URLs without restricting internal or cloud metadata addresses.

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to Command Injection due to the ADMIN_ONLY_OPTIONS protection mechanism being enforced only on core configuration options and not on plugin configuration options. The AntiVirus plugin in plugins/addons/AntiVirus.py at line 75 passes the user-controlled avfile and avargs configuration values directly to subprocess.Popen without validation, and the set_config_value function in core/api/__init__.py at line 271 applies no admin check when writing plugin config entries. A non-admin user with SETTINGS permission can set the AntiVirus avfile path to an arbitrary executable and trigger Remote Code Execution as the pyload process user when a download completes and the scan_file method is invoked.

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to Server-Side Request Forgery due to the absence of URL validation, protocol restriction, or IP blacklisting in the parse_urls API endpoint. The parse_urls function in src/pyload/core/api/__init__.py at line 556 passes the user-supplied url parameter directly to get_url(), which uses pycurl to fetch arbitrary URLs server-side, including file://, gopher://, and dict:// protocols. An authenticated attacker with ADD permission can read local files via the file:// protocol, access cloud metadata endpoints, scan internal network services, and interact with internal services such as Redis or memcached via gopher:// and dict:// protocols.

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to Server-Side Request Forgery due to an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-33992 that fails to validate HTTP redirect targets in the BaseDownloader download path. The SSRF check in src/pyload/plugins/base/downloader.py at lines 335-341 validates only the initial URL hostname, but pycurl is configured with FOLLOWLOCATION=1 and MAXREDIRS=10 in src/pyload/core/network/http/http_request.py at lines 114-115 without any CURLOPT_REDIR_PROTOCOLS restriction, allowing redirect destinations to bypass the filter entirely. An authenticated attacker with ADD permission can submit a URL pointing to an attacker-controlled server that issues a 302 redirect to internal addresses such as cloud metadata endpoints, localhost services, or private network ranges, resulting in the download and storage of sensitive internal resources.

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to Session Cookie Security Downgrade due to an unauthenticated before_request handler that mutates global Flask configuration based on an untrusted request header. The set_session_cookie_secure handler in src/pyload/webui/app/init.py reads the X-Forwarded-Proto header from any HTTP request without validating that the request originates from a trusted proxy, then writes the global SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE key on flask.current_app.config on every request, and because pyLoad uses the multi-threaded Cheroot WSGI server with request_queue_size=512 this creates a race condition where one request's header can influence the Secure flag applied to another user's session cookie. An unauthenticated remote attacker can send crafted requests to either downgrade the Secure flag on other users' session cookies behind a TLS-terminating proxy, enabling cookie exposure over plain HTTP, or cause a session denial-of-service on plain HTTP deployments by forcing the Secure flag on.

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to Improper Session Management due to failure to invalidate or modify active user sessions when an administrator changes a user's permissions. The application continues to honour requests from a still-valid session using its original authorisation state, so the effect of permission changes is not enforced on users who are already logged in. An attacker who retains an authenticated session after an administrator has restricted or removed their permissions can continue to perform actions that the new permissions should prohibit, resulting in unauthorised read and modification of application data.

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to Privilege Escalation due to stale authorisation data being cached in the user session after login. In src/pyload/webui/app/helpers.py, set_session stores the user's role and permission values at login, and parse_permissions, is_authenticated, and login_required subsequently read these cached session values rather than re-checking the database, while set_user_permission in src/pyload/core/api/init.py updates the database without invalidating or refreshing active sessions. An authenticated user whose role or permissions have been revoked by an administrator retains their previous privileges for the remainder of the session (up to the default session_lifetime of 44640 minutes, roughly 31 days), allowing continued execution of privileged actions that should no longer be authorised.

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to Cross-site Scripting (XSS) due to unsanitized interpolation of stored link URLs into a JavaScript template literal that is rendered directly to the DOM. The packages.js template at src/pyload/webui/app/themes/modern/templates/js/packages.js interpolates link.url and six other package fields into a template literal that is subsequently written to the DOM via jQuery's $(div).html(html), with no HTML escaping applied to any of these values before insertion. An authenticated user with Perms.ADD privileges can submit a package link containing a single quote followed by an event-handler payload via /api/add_package; this payload persists in the database and executes in the browser of any operator who opens the /collector or /queue views, allowing the attacker to exfiltrate the administrator's session cookie and take over the account.

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to Improper Authorization due to a hand-maintained admin-only allowlist that omits the security-sensitive general.ssl_verify option from the privileged-write check. The set_config_value() API method in src/pyload/core/api/init.py, gated only by Perms.SETTINGS, rejects writes when the (category, option) tuple appears in ADMIN_ONLY_CORE_OPTIONS but that set does not include ssl_verify, so the value is persisted via config.set() and later consumed by the request factory in src/pyload/core/network/request_factory.py to configure pycurl with SSL_VERIFYPEER=0 and SSL_VERIFYHOST=0. An authenticated non-admin user holding the SETTINGS permission can disable TLS peer and hostname verification for all subsequent outbound requests, allowing an on-path attacker to present forged certificates for any hostname pyload fetches.

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to Information Disclosure due to an incomplete security fix that fails to restrict storage_folder from being set to the Flask session directory. The src/pyload/core/api/__init__.py fix only validates that storage_folder does not reside within PKGDIR or userdir, leaving the Flask session path (/tmp/pyLoad/flask) outside the scope of that check and therefore unprotected. An authenticated attacker with admin privileges can set storage_folder to /tmp/pyLoad/flask and subsequently request GET /files/get/<victim_session_filename> to retrieve session files belonging to other users, resulting in account takeover.

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to Path Traversal due to a lack of sanitization of the package folder name supplied via the API. The set_package_data() function in src/pyload/core/api/init.py accepts the '_folder' key in the data object without any validation, allowing the download folder for a package to be set to an arbitrary absolute or relative filesystem path.

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to Improper Authorization due to a hand-maintained admin-only allowlist that omits the proxy.enabled, proxy.host, proxy.port, and proxy.type fields from the privileged-write check while gating only the proxy credentials. The set_config_value() API method in src/pyload/core/api/init.py, decorated with Perms.SETTINGS, rejects writes only when the (category, option) tuple appears in ADMIN_ONLY_CORE_OPTIONS, which contains proxy.username and proxy.password but not proxy.enabled, proxy.host, proxy.port, or proxy.type; these values are then read by get_proxies() in src/pyload/core/network/request_factory.py and applied to all outbound pycurl requests. An authenticated non-admin user holding the SETTINGS permission can enable proxying and point pyload at an attacker-controlled host, transparently routing every download, captcha fetch, update check, and plugin HTTP call through the attacker.

pyLoad is a free and open-source Download Manager written in pure Python. In version 0.5.0b3.dev89, an authenticated path traversal vulnerability exists in the /json/upload endpoint of pyLoad. By manipulating the filename of an uploaded file, an attacker can traverse out of the intended upload directory, allowing them to write arbitrary files to any location on the system accessible to the pyLoad process. This may lead to: Remote Code Execution (RCE), local privilege escalation, system-wide compromise, persistence, and backdoors. This is fixed in version 0.5.0b3.dev90.

Sensitive Cookie in HTTPS Session Without 'Secure' Attribute in GitHub repository pyload/pyload prior to 0.5.0b3.dev32. The Secure attribute for sensitive cookies in HTTPS sessions is not set, which could cause the user agent to send those cookies in plaintext over an HTTP session. This issue is patched in version 0.5.0b3.dev32.

Affected versions of the pyload-ng package are vulnerable to Remote Code Execution due to unrestricted configuration writes to security-critical settings. The set_config_value() API endpoint in src/pyload/core/api/__init__.py permits users with the non-admin Perms.SETTINGS permission to modify reconnect.script without an allowlist, path restriction, or sanitization, and try_reconnect() in src/pyload/core/managers/thread_manager.py later passes that attacker-controlled path to subprocess.run() after only checking os.path.isfile().

Affected versions of the `pymatgen` package are vulnerable to Remote Code Execution due to the insecure use of the `eval()` function. The `JonesFaithfulTransformation.from_transformation_str()` method processes input using `eval()`, which can execute arbitrary code if the input is untrusted. An attacker can exploit this vulnerability by supplying a maliciously crafted string to the method, leading to the execution of arbitrary commands on the host system.

pymdown-extensions.advisory: Affected versions of the pymdown-extensions package are vulnerable to Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) due to an overly permissive regular expression that treats . as “any character” instead of a literal dot. The pymdownx.blocks.caption module’s figure caption parsing uses the RE_FIG_NUM pattern (r'^(\^)?([1-9][0-9]*(?:.[1-9][0-9]*)*)(?= |$)'), which can exhibit excessive backtracking on certain long inputs.

Pymdown-extensions 10.0 includes a fix for CVE-2023-32309: In affected versions an arbitrary file read is possible when using include file syntax. Any readable file on the host where the plugin is executing may have its content exposed. This can impact any use of Snippets that exposes the use of Snippets to external users. Users unable to upgrade may restrict relative paths by filtering input.
https://github.com/facelessuser/pymdown-extensions/security/advisories/GHSA-jh85-wwv9-24hv

Affected versions of the pymdown-extensions package are vulnerable to Path Traversal due to an incomplete directory-boundary check in the pymdownx.snippets preprocessor that reintroduces a previously patched bypass. The SnippetPreprocessor.get_snippet_path() function in pymdownx/snippets.py enforces the restrict_base_path option using filename.startswith(base) without appending a path separator, so any absolute path that begins with the same literal characters as the configured base directory satisfies the containment check even when the actual directory differs. A markdown author whose content is processed by a build pipeline can include a snippet directive whose resolved path points to a sibling directory sharing the base prefix, causing arbitrary files from outside the intended base to be read and rendered into the generated output and resulting in Information Disclosure of any secrets present on the build host.

pymedusa.advisory: pymedusa is an automatic video library manager for TV Shows. In versions prior 1.0.12 an attacker with access to the web interface can update the git executable path in /config/general/ > advanced settings with arbitrary OS commands. An attacker may exploit this vulnerability to take execute arbitrary OS commands as the user running the pymedusa program. Users are advised to upgrade. There are no known workarounds for this vulnerability.

pymetasploit3.advisory: Affected versions of the pymetasploit3 package are vulnerable to Command Injection due to insufficient neutralization of newline characters in module option values passed to the Metasploit console. The console.run_module_with_output() function forwards option values such as RHOSTS into the console command stream without sanitizing embedded newlines, allowing injected line breaks to terminate the intended command and introduce additional console commands. An attacker who can influence module option values can break out of the intended command structure to execute unintended Metasploit console commands, potentially resulting in arbitrary command execution and the manipulation of Metasploit sessions.

Pyminizip is also vulnerable because it bundles an affected zlib version, and exposes the affected MiniZip code through its compress API.

pympp.advisory: Affected versions of this package are vulnerable to Security Misconfiguration. The application automatically generates and persists a secret key to a `.env` file when one is not explicitly provided. An attacker with read access to the filesystem can extract the auto-generated secret key to forge valid signed tokens or credentials.

Affected versions of this package are vulnerable to Replay Attack. The `expires` value is accepted from the client-controlled `ChargeRequest` body rather than being enforced server-side from the challenge, and the server does not reject credentials after their challenge expiry has passed. An attacker can exploit this by supplying an arbitrarily extended expiry value or replaying a captured credential after its intended expiry window to authenticate with stale or manipulated credentials.

Affected versions of this package are vulnerable to Improper Authentication. The server does not validate that echoed challenge fields (`realm`, `method`, `intent`) match the server-expected values in HTTP and MCP transports. An attacker can exploit this by crafting a response that substitutes challenge fields from a different realm or intent to authenticate against an unintended target.

An attacker can exploit this vulnerability by performing privileged operations beyond their intended access level.

pyp2spec.advisory: Affected versions of the pyp2spec package are vulnerable to Code Injection due to unescaped PyPI package metadata being written directly into generated RPM spec files. The tool inserts fields such as the package summary into the spec without neutralising RPM macro directives, so any macro present in the upstream metadata is evaluated during spec parsing by tools including rpmbuild -bs, rpmbuild --nobuild, and rpm -q --specfile. An attacker who publishes a malicious package, for example via typosquatting or by targeting a package under Fedora review, can achieve arbitrary command execution on the packager's workstation as soon as any rpm tool touches the generated spec, enabling subsequent compromise of dist-git, Koji, and Bodhi credentials.

pypdf.advisory: Affected versions of the pypdf package are vulnerable to Denial of Service (DoS) due to missing cycle detection when following /Prev pointers in the PDF cross-reference chain. The PdfReader() parsing flow in pypdf/_reader.py calls _read_xref_tables_and_trailers(), which iterates with a while startxref is not None loop and repeatedly follows /Prev offsets without tracking previously visited xref locations, allowing a circular reference to keep the loop running forever.

Affected versions of the pypdf package are vulnerable to Denial of Service (DoS) due to unbounded decompression of FlateDecode-encoded streams that can exhaust memory. The `pypdf.filters.decompress` function used by the `FlateDecode` filter, invoked by `PdfReader` when parsing cross-reference streams via `_reader._read_pdf15_xref_stream` and when accessing other content streams, failed to enforce a maximum decompressed output length. An attacker can exploit this by providing a crafted PDF whose cross-reference stream chains FlateDecode filters so that simply opening the file with `PdfReader` triggers excessive memory allocation, leading to process termination or service unavailability without authentication.

Affected versions of the pypdf package are vulnerable to Denial of Service (DoS) due to an infinite loop in the DCTDecode inline image parser when the end-of-image marker is missing. The extract_inline_DCT function in pypdf/generic/_image_inline.py reads bytes from an inline DCT image while parsing a page’s content stream and, for malformed JPEG data lacking the 0xFFD9 EOI marker, fails to reach a termination condition, permitting unbounded iteration.

Affected versions of the pypdf package are vulnerable to Denial of Service (DoS) due to unbounded decompression of LZWDecode streams in page content that lack an enforced output-size limit. The LZWDecode filter path in pypdf/filters.py invoked _LzwCodec.decode from pypdf/_codecs/_codecs.py without bounding the decompressed output, permitting extremely high expansion ratios during decode() and uncontrolled memory allocation.

Affected versions of the pypdf package are vulnerable to Denial of Service due to improper handling of XML entity declarations in XMP metadata parsing. Crafted PDF files containing manipulated XMP metadata with recursive or excessively large entity declarations can trigger unbounded memory consumption when the metadata is parsed. An attacker can supply a specially crafted PDF document to exhaust available memory on the system processing it, resulting in service disruption.

Affected versions of the pypdf package are vulnerable to Denial of Service due to insufficient validation of size fields when parsing PDF cross-reference streams and object streams. When pypdf encounters a cross-reference stream with an incorrectly large /Size value or an object stream with an incorrectly large /N value, the parser performs work proportional to the declared size rather than the actual data present, leading to excessively long runtimes. An attacker who can supply a crafted PDF to an application that parses it with pypdf can trigger these inflated iterations to consume CPU time and delay or block processing.

Affected versions of the pypdf package are vulnerable to Denial of Service due to excessive iteration driven by an unvalidated trailer /Size value when loading a PDF in incremental mode. The incremental parsing path trusts the trailer /Size entry to determine how many cross-reference entries to process and performs work proportional to that value without bounding it against the actual file contents, so a crafted PDF declaring a disproportionately large /Size causes a loop to run for a long time. An attacker who can induce a victim to open a crafted PDF with pypdf in incremental mode can exploit this to cause excessive processing time on the host, degrading availability through prolonged runtime of the parsing operation.

Affected versions of the pypdf package are vulnerable to Denial of Service due to memory allocation based on untrusted predictor parameters when decoding streams compressed with the FlateDecode filter. When a stream declares a /Predictor value other than 1, the decoder sizes its working buffers from the accompanying predictor parameters without bounding them against the actual stream contents, so a crafted PDF that declares very large predictor parameter values causes a disproportionately large memory allocation during decompression. An attacker who can cause a victim to process a malicious PDF with pypdf can exploit this to exhaust the host's available RAM, resulting in a Denial of Service on the processing system.

Affected versions of the pypdf package are vulnerable to Denial of Service due to memory allocation based on untrusted image dimension values when decoding PDF images compressed with the FlateDecode filter. The decoder trusts the Width and Height metadata for a FlateDecode-compressed image object and allocates a buffer of the corresponding size without bounding the requested size, so a crafted PDF that declares very large dimensions for such an image causes a disproportionately large memory allocation during access. An attacker who can cause a victim to open or process a malicious PDF with pypdf can exploit this to exhaust available RAM on the processing host, resulting in a Denial of Service.

Affected versions of the pypdf package are vulnerable to Denial of Service (DoS) due to insufficient limiting of memory usage when decoding LZWDecode content streams. The pypdf.filters LZWDecode implementation allows attacker-controlled page content streams to be decompressed without an effective maximum output size, so a single highly compressed stream can expand to roughly 1 GB of in-memory data during parsing.

Affected versions of the pypdf package are vulnerable to Denial of Service (DoS) due to unbounded Root-object recovery work driven by an attacker-controlled /Size trailer value when /Root is missing in non-strict mode. In pypdf’s PdfReader non-strict parsing path, omitting the trailer /Root entry while setting a huge/Size causes the reader to attempt to access object numbers up to the /Size limit (mitigated in later versions via the root_object_recovery_limit control), resulting in potentially long runtimes on invalid PDFs.

Affected versions of the pypdf package are vulnerable to Denial of Service (DoS) due to inefficient cross-reference table rebuilding when handling malformed startxref data in non-strict mode. In pypdf._reader.PdfReader._rebuild_xref_table(), the non-strict recovery path scans the entire PDF buffer with a re.finditer() pattern to rediscover obj markers, which can take excessively long on inputs dominated by whitespace.

Affected versions of the pypdf package are vulnerable to Denial of Service (DoS) due to missing cycle detection when traversing PDF outlines/bookmarks. The PdfReader.outline property calls _get_outline() in pypdf/_doc_common.py, which iterates through outline nodes (including /Next and nested /First entries) without reliably tracking visited nodes, allowing a crafted cyclic outline structure to trigger an infinite loop.

Affected versions of the pypdf package are vulnerable to Denial of Service (DoS) due to unbounded processing of unusually large /ToUnicode font streams in crafted PDFs. When pypdf parses a font’s /ToUnicode entry (for example during text extraction), it can iterate over and allocate data for exceptionally large values without sufficient limits, resulting in long runtimes and high memory consumption.

Affected versions of the pypdf package are vulnerable to Denial of Service (DoS) due to an infinite loop when traversing cyclic outline tree references. The pypdf.generic._data_structures.TreeObject.children() iterator follows the /First → /Next chain until /Last without reliably detecting cycles, so a crafted outline structure can prevent the loop’s exit condition from ever being reached.

Affected versions of the pypdf package are vulnerable to Denial of Service (DoS) due to unbounded byte-by-byte recovery decompression on malformed /FlateDecode streams. In pypdf/filters.py, the decompress logic can fall back to iterating over the compressed stream one byte at a time and repeatedly calling zlib.decompressobj(...).decompress(...), which can take an excessively long time when the input stream is intentionally malformed and triggers recovery behaviour.

Affected versions of the pypdf package are vulnerable to Denial of Service (DoS) due to uncontrolled memory allocation during XFA stream decoding compressed with /FlateDecode. The issue occurs when the xfa property is accessed on a PdfReader or PdfWriter, causing pypdf’s FlateDecode stream handling to expand attacker-controlled compressed data without sufficient resource limits.

Affected versions of the pypdf package are vulnerable to Denial of Service (DoS) due to uncontrolled memory allocation while decoding RunLengthDecode-compressed PDF content streams. The issue occurs in pypdf/filters.py where RunLengthDecode.decode() expands attacker-controlled run-length segments into an in-memory buffer without an effective maximum output-length limit in affected releases.

Affected versions of the pypdf package are vulnerable to Denial of Service (DoS) due to inefficient algorithmic complexity in the ASCIIHexDecode stream decoding. The pypdf.filters.ASCIIHexDecode.decode method in pypdf/filters.py performs per-byte parsing with repeated buffer concatenation when converting hex pairs into output bytes, which can cause disproportionate runtime on large /ASCIIHexDecode streams.

Affected versions of the pypdf package are vulnerable to Denial of Service (DoS) due to unbounded memory allocation based on attacker-controlled stream length values. When pypdf parses a PDF content stream, it trusts a large /Length value even when the underlying stream data is much smaller, leading to excessive memory consumption during stream processing.

Affected versions of the pypdf package are vulnerable to Denial of Service (DoS) due to inefficient decoding of array-based streams. In PageObject._get_contents_as_bytes(), pypdf decodes array-based /Contents streams by joining the decoded data from each entry, which can cause excessive runtime and memory consumption when the array contains a very large number of stream objects.

Affected versions of the pypdf package are vulnerable to Denial of Service (DoS) due to an infinite loop caused by improper error handling in non-strict parsing mode. The vulnerability is in DictionaryObject.read_from_stream, where malformed PDF input can trigger recovery handling for recursion and filter limit errors that should terminate parsing instead of continuing indefinitely.

Pypdf 3.9.0 includes a fix for CVE-2023-36464: In affected versions an attacker may craft a PDF which leads to an infinite loop if '__parse_content_stream' is executed. That is, for example, the case if the user extracted text from such a PDF. This issue was introduced in pull request #969 and resolved in pull request #1828. Users unable to upgrade may modify the line 'while peek not in (b"\r", b"\n")' in 'pypdf/generic/_data_structures.py' to 'while peek not in (b"\r", b"\n", b"")'.
https://github.com/py-pdf/pypdf/pull/1828
https://github.com/py-pdf/pypdf/security/advisories/GHSA-4vvm-4w3v-6mr8

Pypdf 3.17.0 includes a fix for CVE-2023-46250: An attacker who uses a vulnerability present in versions 3.7.0 through 3.16.4 can craft a PDF which leads to an infinite loop. This infinite loop blocks the current process and can utilize a single core of the CPU by 100%. It does not affect memory usage. That is, for example, the case when the pypdf-user manipulates an incoming malicious PDF e.g. by merging it with another PDF or by adding annotations. As a workaround, apply the patch manually by modifying 'pypdf/generic/_data_structures.py'.
https://github.com/py-pdf/pypdf/security/advisories/GHSA-wjcc-cq79-p63f

pypxe.advisory: Affected versions of the PyPXE package are vulnerable to Buffer Overflow due to improper packet length validation in the `tftp` module. The `handle` function in the `tftp` module attempts to unpack the opcode using `struct.unpack('!H', self.message[:2])` without verifying that the packet length is at least two bytes, which can lead to buffer overflow. A remote attacker can exploit this by sending a specially crafted undersized packet to the PyPXE `tftp` handle function, causing the TFTP component to crash and resulting in a Denial of Service.

pyquokka.advisory: Affected versions of the pyquokka package are vulnerable to Deserialization of Untrusted Data due to unsafe use of pickle.loads on client-supplied Flight action bodies. The FlightServer.do_action method in pyquokka/flight.py (line 283) deserializes unvalidated data, with additional unsafe use of pickle.loads in cache_garbage_collect, do_put, and do_get, enabling arbitrary object construction.

pyquorum.advisory: Affected versions of the pyquorum package are vulnerable to a Timing Side-Channel Attack due to the mul_mod function implementing multiplication via a binary expansion loop whose execution time varies with the Hamming weight of the second operand. This non-constant-time behaviour in mul_mod leaks information about operand values through measurable timing differences during secret-sharing operations. An attacker who can measure the execution time of these operations, such as through a remote service interface, could progressively recover the values of individual shares and ultimately reconstruct the protected secret.

pyramid.advisory: Pyramid 0.4.2 changes the default paster template generator to use ``Paste#http`` server rather than ``PasteScript#cherrpy`` server.  The cherrypy server has a  security risk in it when ``REMOTE_USER`` is trusted by the downstream application.

In pyramid before 1.0a3, the pylons_* paster template used the same string (``your_app_secret_string``) for the ``session.secret`` setting in the generated ``development.ini``.  This was a security risk if left unchanged in a project that used one of the templates to produce production applications.  It now uses a randomly generated string.
https://github.com/Pylons/pyramid/commit/7bd14cbfb396bdb1e892ef0b9d51619c78ae368f

The default Mako renderer in pyramid 1.1a1 is configured to escape all HTML in expression tags. This is intended to help prevent XSS attacks caused by rendering unsanitized input from users. To revert this behavior in user's templates, they need to filter the expression through the 'n' filter. For example, ${ myhtml | n }. See <https://github.com/Pylons/pyramid/issues/193>.
The AuthTktAuthenticationPolicy in pyramid before 1.3a1 did not use a timing-attack-aware string comparator.  See https://github.com/Pylons/pyramid/pull/320 for more info.

In pyramid 1.4a4 the ``pyramid.authentication.AuthTktAuthenticationPolicy`` has been updated to support newer hashing algorithms such as ``sha512``. Existing applications should consider updating if possible for improved security over the default md5 hashing.

Pyramid 1.6a1 prevents timing attacks in 'AuthTktCookieHelper' and 'SignedCookieSessionFactory' classes by using the stdlib's 'hmac.compare_digest' if it is available (such as in Python 2.7.7+ and 3.3+). 
https://github.com/Pylons/pyramid/pull/1457

Pyramid 1.6a1 prevents timing attacks against CSRF tokens.
https://github.com/Pylons/pyramid/pull/1574

pyramid before 1.6a2 isn't sanitising JSONP callbacks correctly, see CVE-2014-4671.
https://github.com/Pylons/pyramid/commit/67efda77a878450c217b90370e1a47e2d35d772a

Pyramid 2.0.2 includes a fix for CVE-2023-40587: A path traversal vulnerability in Pyramid versions 2.0.0 and 2.0.1 impacts users of Python 3.11 that are using a Pyramid static view with a full filesystem path and have a 'index.html' file that is located exactly one directory above the location of the static view's file system path. No further path traversal exists, and the only file that could be disclosed accidentally is 'index.html'. Pyramid version 2.0.2 rejects any path that contains a null-byte out of caution. While valid in directory/file names, we would strongly consider it a mistake to use null-bytes in naming files/directories. Secondly, Python 3.11, and 3.12 has fixed the underlying issue in 'os.path.normpath' to no longer truncate on the first '0x00' found, returning the behavior to pre-3.11 Python. Fixes will be available in:Python 3.12.0rc2 and 3.11.5. Some workarounds are available. Use a version of Python 3 that is not affected, downgrade to Python 3.10 series temporarily, or wait until Python 3.11.5 is released and upgrade to the latest version of Python 3.11 series.
https://github.com/Pylons/pyramid/security/advisories/GHSA-j8g2-6fc7-q8f8

PySAML2 before 5.0.0 does not check that the signature in a SAML document is enveloped and thus signature wrapping is effective, i.e., it is affected by XML Signature Wrapping (XSW). The signature information and the node/object that is signed can be in different places and thus the signature verification will succeed, but the wrong data will be used. This specifically affects the verification of assertion that have been signed.

PySAML2 is a pure python implementation of SAML Version 2 Standard. PySAML2 before 6.5.0 has an improper verification of cryptographic signature vulnerability. Users of pysaml2 that use the default CryptoBackendXmlSec1 backend and need to verify signed SAML documents are impacted. PySAML2 does not ensure that a signed SAML document is correctly signed. The default CryptoBackendXmlSec1 backend is using the xmlsec1 binary to verify the signature of signed SAML documents, but by default xmlsec1 accepts any type of key found within the given document. xmlsec1 needs to be configured explicitly to only use only _x509 certificates_ for the verification process of the SAML document signature. This is fixed in PySAML2 6.5.0. See CVE-2021-21239.

PySAML2 is a pure python implementation of SAML Version 2 Standard. PySAML2 before 6.5.0 has an improper verification of cryptographic signature vulnerability. All users of pysaml2 that need to validate signed SAML documents are impacted. The vulnerability is a variant of XML Signature wrapping because it did not validate the SAML document against an XML schema. This allowed invalid XML documents to be processed and such a document can trick pysaml2 with a wrapped signature. This is fixed in PySAML2 6.5.0. See CVE-2021-21238.

pyspark.advisory: Prior to Spark 2.3.3, in certain situations Spark would write user data to local disk unencrypted, even if spark.io.encryption.enabled=true. This includes cached blocks that are fetched to disk (controlled by spark.maxRemoteBlockSizeFetchToMem); in SparkR, using parallelize; in Pyspark, using broadcast and parallelize; and use of python udfs.

Affected versions of the Apache Spark package are vulnerable to Improper Input Validation due to insufficient restrictions on classpath configurations. The vulnerability exists because applications can specify arbitrary configuration-related classes on the classpath, circumventing the intended privilege limitations imposed by the 'proxy-user' setting. An attacker can exploit this by submitting a malicious application that includes custom classpath entries, allowing execution of code with the privileges of the submitting user rather than the restricted proxy-user, potentially compromising system security.

** UNSUPPORTED WHEN ASSIGNED ** The Apache Spark UI offers the possibility to enable ACLs via the configuration option spark.acls.enable. With an authentication filter, this checks whether a user has access permissions to view or modify the application. If ACLs are enabled, a code path in HttpSecurityFilter can allow someone to perform impersonation by providing an arbitrary user name. A malicious user might then be able to reach a permission check function that will ultimately build a Unix shell command based on their input, and execute it. This will result in arbitrary shell command execution as the user Spark is currently running as. This issue was disclosed earlier as CVE-2022-33891, but incorrectly claimed version 3.1.3 (which has since gone EOL) would not be affected. NOTE: This vulnerability only affects products that are no longer supported by the maintainer. Users are recommended to upgrade to a supported version of Apache Spark, such as version 3.4.0.

In Apache Spark 2.1.0 to 2.1.2, 2.2.0 to 2.2.1, and 2.3.0, it's possible for a malicious user to construct a URL pointing to a Spark cluster's UI's job and stage info pages, and if a user can be tricked into accessing the URL, can be used to cause script to execute and expose information from the user's view of the Spark UI. While some browsers like recent versions of Chrome and Safari are able to block this type of attack, current versions of Firefox (and possibly others) do not.

In Apache Spark before 2.2.0, it is possible for an attacker to take advantage of a user's trust in the server to trick them into visiting a link that points to a shared Spark cluster and submits data including MHTML to the Spark master, or history server. This data, which could contain a script, would then be reflected back to the user and could be evaluated and executed by MS Windows-based clients. It is not an attack on Spark itself, but on the user, who may then execute the script inadvertently when viewing elements of the Spark web UIs.

In Apache Spark 2.4.5 and earlier, a standalone resource manager's master may be configured to require authentication (spark.authenticate) via a shared secret. When enabled, however, a specially-crafted RPC to the master can succeed in starting an application's resources on the Spark cluster, even without the shared key. This can be leveraged to execute shell commands on the host machine. This does not affect Spark clusters using other resource managers (YARN, Mesos, etc).

Apache Spark supports end-to-end encryption of RPC connections via "spark.authenticate" and "spark.network.crypto.enabled". In versions 3.1.2 and earlier, it uses a bespoke mutual authentication protocol that allows for full encryption key recovery. After an initial interactive attack, this would allow someone to decrypt plaintext traffic offline. Note that this does not affect security mechanisms controlled by "spark.authenticate.enableSaslEncryption", "spark.io.encryption.enabled", "spark.ssl", "spark.ui.strictTransportSecurity". Update to Apache Spark 3.1.3 or later

Pyspark before 3.1.3, equal or above 3.2.0 and below 3.2.2 are vulnerable to arbitrary command execution. This vulnerability stems from a flaw in the Utils.unpack method, where a filename controlled by a malicious user is not properly escaped by Hadoop's unTar function before it is passed to a shell command.
https://github.com/apache/spark/pull/35946/commits/7b16ba4ab792f6e63f4f1ad0ec5bba245a01a721

A stored cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in Apache Spark 3.2.1 and earlier, and 3.3.0, allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the web browser of a user, by including a malicious payload into the logs which would be returned in logs rendered in the UI.

In Apache Spark 1.6.0 until 2.1.1, the launcher API performs unsafe deserialization of data received by its socket. This makes applications launched programmatically using the launcher API potentially vulnerable to arbitrary code execution by an attacker with access to any user account on the local machine. It does not affect apps run by spark-submit or spark-shell. The attacker would be able to execute code as the user that ran the Spark application. Users are encouraged to update to version 2.2.0 or later.

In Apache Spark 1.0.0 to 2.1.2, 2.2.0 to 2.2.1, and 2.3.0, when using PySpark or SparkR, it's possible for a different local user to connect to the Spark application and impersonate the user running the Spark application.

When using PySpark , it's possible for a different local user to connect to the Spark application and impersonate the user running the Spark application. This affects versions 1.x, 2.0.x, 2.1.x, 2.2.0 to 2.2.2, and 2.3.0 to 2.3.1.

pyspector.advisory: Affected versions of the pyspector package are vulnerable to Cross-site Scripting (XSS) due to unsanitized flagged code snippets being interpolated into generated HTML reports. The HTML report generator inserts JavaScript-containing content from scanned Python files, including strings passed to eval(), into the report without neutralizing script content, causing the payload to execute when the report is opened in a browser.

Affected versions of the pyspector package are vulnerable to Arbitrary Code Execution due to incomplete validation of plugin code. The validate_plugin_code() function in plugin_system.py relies on the resolve_name() helper during AST-based security checks, but resolve_name() only handles ast.Name and ast.Attribute nodes, so indirect calls such as getattr(os, 'system') are not resolved and the dangerous call check is skipped.

Affected versions of the pyspector package are vulnerable to Sandbox Bypass due to an incomplete blocklist in the AST-based plugin security validator. PluginSecurity.validate_plugin_code enforces a fatal_calls set of known-dangerous identifiers such as eval, exec, os.system, and subprocess.Popen, but does not detect importlib.import_module, class.mro dunder traversal, ctypes, builtins dictionary access, types.CodeType, or aliased and transitive imports, allowing these constructs to reach arbitrary built-ins and native code without matching any blocked name. An attacker who can supply a plugin file that is installed with the --trust flag can bypass the validator and achieve arbitrary code execution with the full privileges of the PySpector process when the plugin is executed.

python.advisory: A vulnerability classified as problematic was found in Python 2.7.13. This vulnerability affects unknown code of the component pgAdmin4. The manipulation leads to uncontrolled search path. The attack can be initiated remotely. The exploit has been disclosed to the public and may be used.

NOTE: this vulnerability reportedly exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2008-2315.

Python 2.5.2 and earlier allows context-dependent attackers to execute arbitrary code via multiple vectors that cause a negative size value to be provided to the PyString_FromStringAndSize function, which allocates less memory than expected when assert() is disabled and triggers a buffer overflow.

Python 2.7.15 includes a fix for CVE-2018-1000030: Python 2.7.14 is vulnerable to a Heap-Buffer-Overflow as well as a Heap-Use-After-Free. Python versions prior to 2.7.14 may also be vulnerable and it appears that Python 2.7.17 and prior may also be vulnerable however this has not been confirmed. The vulnerability lies when multiply threads are handling large amounts of data. In both cases there is essentially a race condition that occurs. For the Heap-Buffer-Overflow, Thread 2 is creating the size for a buffer, but Thread1 is already writing to the buffer without knowing how much to write. So when a large amount of data is being processed, it is very easy to cause memory corruption using a Heap-Buffer-Overflow. As for the Use-After-Free, Thread3->Malloc->Thread1->Free's->Thread2-Re-uses-Free'd Memory. The PSRT has stated that this is not a security vulnerability due to the fact that the attacker must be able to run code, however in some situations, such as function as a service, this vulnerability can potentially be used by an attacker to violate a trust boundary, as such the DWF feels this issue deserves a CVE.
https://bugs.python.org/issue31530

Python before versions 2.7.15, 3.4.9, 3.5.6rc1, 3.6.5rc1 and 3.7.0 is vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking in pop3lib's apop() method. An attacker could use this flaw to cause denial of service.

This attack appear to be exploitable via Passage of unfiltered user input to the function.

https://bugs.python.org/issue34623

Python versions 2.7.16, 3.4.10, 3.5.7, 3.6.7, 3.7.1 and 3.8.0 include a fix for CVE-2019-17514: Library/glob.html in the Python 2 and 3 documentation before 2016 has potentially misleading information about whether sorting occurs, as demonstrated by irreproducible cancer-research results. NOTE: the effects of this documentation cross application domains, and thus it is likely that security-relevant code elsewhere is affected. This issue is not a Python implementation bug, and there are no reports that NMR researchers were specifically relying on library/glob.html. In other words, because the older documentation stated "finds all the pathnames matching a specified pattern according to the rules used by the Unix shell," one might have incorrectly inferred that the sorting that occurs in a Unix shell also occurred for glob.glob. There is a workaround in newer versions of Willoughby nmr-data_compilation-p2.py and nmr-data_compilation-p3.py, which call sort() directly.
https://bugs.python.org/issue33275
https://www.vice.com/en/article/zmjwda/a-code-glitch-may-have-caused-errors-in-more-than-100-published-studies

A specially crafted X509 certificate can cause a NULL pointer dereference, resulting in a denial of service. An attacker can initiate or accept TLS connections using crafted certificates to trigger this vulnerability.

Python versions 2.7.16, 3.4.10, 3.5.7, 3.6.9 and 3.7.3 include a fix for CVE-2018-20852: http.cookiejar.DefaultPolicy.domain_return_ok in Lib/http/cookiejar.py in Python before 3.7.3 does not correctly validate the domain: it can be tricked into sending existing cookies to the wrong server. An attacker may abuse this flaw by using a server with a hostname that has another valid hostname as a suffix (e.g., pythonicexample.com to steal cookies for example.com). When a program uses http.cookiejar.DefaultPolicy and tries to do an HTTP connection to an attacker-controlled server, existing cookies can be leaked to the attacker.

Python versions 2.7.17, 3.5.10, 3.6.10 and 3.7.5 include a fix for CVE-2019-16935: The documentation XML-RPC server in Python through 2.7.16, 3.x through 3.6.9, and 3.7.x through 3.7.4 has XSS via the server_title field. This occurs in Lib/DocXMLRPCServer.py in Python 2.x, and in Lib/xmlrpc/server.py in Python 3.x. If set_server_title is called with untrusted input, arbitrary JavaScript can be delivered to clients that visit the http URL for this server.

Python versions 2.7.17, 3.5.7, 3.6.9 and 3.7.3 include a fix for CVE-2019-9636: Python 2.7.x through 2.7.16 and 3.x through 3.7.2 is affected by Improper Handling of Unicode Encoding (with an incorrect netloc) during NFKC normalization. The impact is information disclosure (credentials, cookies, etc. that are cached against a given hostname). The affected components are urllib.parse.urlsplit and urllib.parse.urlparse. The attack vector is a specially crafted URL that could be incorrectly parsed to locate cookies or authentication data and send that information to a different host.
https://bugs.python.org/issue36216

Python versions 3.8.0b2, 3.7.4, 3.6.10, 3.5.8 and 2.7.17 include a fix for CVE-2019-10160: A security regression of CVE-2019-9636 was discovered in python since commit d537ab0ff9767ef024f26246899728f0116b1ec3 affecting versions 2.7, 3.5, 3.6, 3.7 and from v3.8.0a4 through v3.8.0b1, which still allows an attacker to exploit CVE-2019-9636 by abusing the user and password parts of a URL. When an application parses user-supplied URLs to store cookies, authentication credentials, or other kind of information, it is possible for an attacker to provide specially crafted URLs to make the application locate host-related information (e.g. cookies, authentication data) and send them to a different host than where it should, unlike if the URLs had been correctly parsed. The result of an attack may vary based on the application.
https://bugs.python.org/issue36742

A defect was discovered in the Python “ssl” module where there is a memory race condition with the ssl.SSLContext methods “cert_store_stats()” and “get_ca_certs()”. The race condition can be triggered if the methods are called at the same time as certificates are loaded into the SSLContext, such as during the TLS handshake with a certificate directory configured.

An issue was found in CPython 3.12.0 `subprocess` module on POSIX platforms. The issue was fixed in CPython 3.12.1 and does not affect other stable releases. When using the `extra_groups=` parameter with an empty list as a value (ie `extra_groups=[]`) the logic regressed to not call `setgroups(0, NULL)` before calling `exec()`, thus not dropping the original processes' groups before starting the new process. There is no issue when the parameter isn't used or when any value is used besides an empty list. This issue only impacts CPython processes run with sufficient privilege to make the `setgroups` system call (typically `root`).

In Python before 3.10.3 on Windows, local users can gain privileges because the search path is inadequately secured. The installer may allow a local attacker to add user-writable directories to the system search path. To exploit, an administrator must have installed Python for all users and enabled PATH entries. A non-administrative user can trigger a repair that incorrectly adds user-writable paths into PATH, enabling search-path hijacking of other users and system services. This affects Python (CPython) through 3.7.12, 3.8.x through 3.8.12, 3.9.x through 3.9.10, and 3.10.x through 3.10.2.
